lesson.title: Decisions Inside Decisions
lesson.summary: A nested conditional places one if, if-else, or elif statement inside the body of another, letting a program make a second decision only after the first has already narrowed down which situation applies.
lesson.body:
A nested conditional is simply a conditional statement, whether if, if-else, or an elif chain, written inside the body of another conditional statement. Instead of one flat decision, the program makes a decision, and then, only within one specific branch of that decision, makes a second, more specific decision. Nesting is what lets a program express "first check this broad category, and once we know we're in that category, check something narrower" without inventing any new syntax, it is entirely built from the elif and if-else statements already covered, just written at increasing levels of indentation.

Trace this example, which checks both whether someone can vote and whether they are registered:

age = 20
is_registered = False
if age >= 18:
    if is_registered:
        print("You can vote")
    else:
        print("Register to vote")
else:
    print("Too young to vote")

Python first evaluates age >= 18. With age at 20, that is True, so control enters the outer if block rather than the outer else. Inside that block sits an entire second if-else statement, checking is_registered. Since is_registered is False, the inner condition is False, so Python runs the inner else, printing "Register to vote". Notice the outer else, "Too young to vote", is never even considered, because the outer condition was already True; nesting means the inner conditional only exists, and only gets evaluated, within the specific branch that contains it.

Each additional level of nesting adds one more indentation level, and Python uses that indentation to know exactly which conditional a given line belongs to. It is easy, especially with three or four levels of nesting, to lose track of which else pairs with which if, so it is worth checking, for every else or elif in a nested block, that it lines up visually with the if it belongs to. This is also where the earlier logical operators and De Morgan's laws become genuinely useful: the two-level nested example above could be flattened into a single condition using and, as if age >= 18 and is_registered:, which often reads more clearly than two levels of nesting when the inner check has no separate else of its own.

Nested conditionals are not a new control flow structure, they are a direct consequence of the fact that an if, if-else, or elif body can contain any valid statement, including another conditional statement. Recognizing that gives you a useful rule of thumb: reach for nesting when the inner decision only makes sense in the context of the outer one, and reach for a combined boolean expression with and or or when the two conditions are really being checked together rather than one depending on the other.

Nesting can also go more than two levels deep, and an inner conditional can itself be an elif chain rather than a simple if-else, so the two ideas combine freely. As the nesting gets deeper, each level adds its own indentation, and it becomes easy to lose track of which block a given else belongs to just by eyeballing it. A reliable way to check your own nested code is to read only one indentation level at a time, confirming that every else or elif at that level pairs with the if directly above it at the same indentation, before worrying about what happens further inside.
